description: The major scale (Ionian mode) — the default "happy", stable scale of Western music. Fits naturally over a maj or maj7 chord built on its root. Used across virtually every genre for pop, folk, and country progressions; the reference point every other mode is defined relative to

The natural minor scale (Aeolian mode) — the default dark, melancholic scale, and the relative minor of the major scale sharing the same key signature. Fits naturally over a min or min7 chord built on its root. Extremely common across rock, pop, folk, and reggae for a sadder or more serious feel than major

The dorian mode — a minor scale with a raised sixth compared to natural minor, giving it a brighter, less resolved minor colour. Fits naturally over a min or min7 chord. Common in funk, jazz, and modal rock (e.g. extended vamps on a single minor chord), favored where a minor sound shouldn't feel too heavy or sad

The phrygian mode — a minor scale with a flattened second, giving it a tense, exotic, or Spanish-flamenco character. Fits over a min chord. Used in flamenco, metal, and some Latin styles where a darker, more unsettled minor colour is wanted than dorian or natural minor provide

The lydian mode — a major scale with a raised fourth, giving it a bright, floating, slightly unresolved quality compared to plain major. Fits over a maj or maj7 chord. Common in film-score and progressive rock/jazz contexts for a dreamy or ethereal major sound; less common in mainstream pop

The mixolydian mode — a major scale with a flattened seventh, giving it a bluesy, less resolved quality than plain major. Fits naturally over a dominant 7 chord. Core to blues, rock, and funk, especially over the I chord in a blues progression or any dominant-seventh vamp. Also a key jazz scale, used over dominant 7 chords in ii-V-I progressions and applied-dominant vamps

The locrian mode — a minor scale with both a flattened second and flattened fifth, making it the most unstable and dissonant mode with no true point of rest. Fits over a diminished chord. Rarely used as a basis for a full progression; mostly relevant as a brief passing colour over a vii° or other diminished chord

The major pentatonic scale — the major scale with the fourth and seventh removed, leaving no half-steps and a very consonant, easy-to-use sound. Extremely common in pop, country, folk, and rock for simple, singable basslines and riffs that rarely clash with the underlying harmony

The minor pentatonic scale — the natural minor scale with the second and sixth removed, leaving a simple, consonant, half-step-free sound. The default scale for rock, blues, and pop guitar riffs and basslines; forms the basis of the blues scale with one note added

The blues scale — the minor pentatonic scale with an added flattened fifth (the "blue note"), giving it a gritty, expressive, dissonant edge. The signature scale of blues and blues-rock, typically played over a I7-IV7-V7 blues progression regardless of the underlying chord quality

The harmonic minor scale — natural minor with a raised seventh, creating a strong pull back to the tonic (unlike natural minor) and a distinctive augmented second gap between the sixth and seventh degrees. Fits over a min or min(maj7) chord. Common in classical and neoclassical metal, and used in jazz over the V7 of a minor ii-V-i for a stronger resolution to the tonic than natural minor gives; also the parent scale for several exotic-sounding modes, most notably phrygian dominant

Phrygian dominant — the fifth mode of harmonic minor, combining a flattened second with a major third for an exotic, tense, unresolved sound. Fits over a dominant 7 (often 7b9) chord, especially a V chord resolving to a minor i. Core to flamenco, Middle Eastern and Balkan music, and klezmer (where it's called Freygish); also used in neoclassical metal soloing
